subtopic_detail: First-line investigation of a swollen calf in pregnancy
stem:
A 28-year-old woman at 26 weeks in her second pregnancy comes to the day assessment unit with two days of left calf pain that is worse when she walks to the letterbox. She has had no chest tightness, breathlessness or cough.

On examination the left calf measures 3 cm greater in circumference than the right at 10 cm below the tibial tuberosity, and there is tenderness along the medial calf with mild pitting over the ankle. She has no personal or family history of venous thromboembolism.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88/min, BP 112/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius; foetal heart rate 142/min
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count and electrolytes within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial investigation?

options.text: Plasma D-dimer, proceeding to leg imaging only if the reported level is raised
options.rationale: D-dimer rises progressively through normal pregnancy, so a raised result adds nothing and a low result has not been validated to exclude clot in pregnant women; using it as the gate delays definitive imaging. (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: Venous thromboembolism in pregnancy)
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: Venous thromboembolism in pregnancy

options.text: Contrast venography of the left leg performed with abdominal shielding in place
options.rationale: Venography is invasive, uses iodinated contrast and ionising radiation, and has been replaced by ultrasound as the first test; it is now reserved for the rare case where ultrasound cannot answer the question. (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: Venous thromboembolism in pregnancy)
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: Venous thromboembolism in pregnancy

options.text: Compression duplex ultrasound of the left leg veins performed the same day
options.rationale: Compression ultrasound is the first-line test for suspected deep vein thrombosis in pregnancy: no radiation, immediately available, and directly images the femoral and popliteal segments where pregnancy-associated clot usually sits. (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: Venous thromboembolism in pregnancy)
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: Venous thromboembolism in pregnancy
Queensland Clinical Guidelines: Venous thromboembolism (VTE) prophylaxis in pregnancy and the puerperium

options.text: Computed tomography pulmonary angiogram of the chest using a reduced-dose protocol
options.rationale: Chest imaging answers a different question and she has no respiratory symptoms or signs; it is indicated when pulmonary embolism is suspected, not for isolated unilateral calf findings. (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: Venous thromboembolism in pregnancy)
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: Venous thromboembolism in pregnancy

options.text: Magnetic resonance venography of the pelvic veins and both femoral segments
options.rationale: Magnetic resonance venography is a second-line study kept for suspected iliac vein clot when leg ultrasound is negative but symptoms persist; it is not the initial test for a symptomatic calf. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guidelines: Venous thromboembolism (VTE) prophylaxis in pregnancy and the puerperium)
source_refs: Queensland Clinical Guidelines: Venous thromboembolism (VTE) prophylaxis in pregnancy and the puerperium

explanation.summary: Venous thromboembolism remains a leading direct cause of maternal death in Australia, and most of those deaths follow a clot that was symptomatic before it was fatal. Pregnancy raises factors VIII, VII and fibrinogen, reduces protein S and causes venous stasis from the second trimester, so the pre-test probability of clot in a swollen painful calf is far higher than in a non-pregnant woman of the same age. Around 80 to 90 per cent of pregnancy deep vein thrombosis is left-sided and proximal, because the right iliac artery crosses and compresses the left iliac vein. Ultrasound is therefore both safe and high-yield as the opening move. In context, the decision a Year 4 student is expected to make is to image rather than to risk-score a pregnant leg.
key_points: Compression duplex ultrasound is the first-line investigation for suspected deep vein thrombosis in pregnancy.
D-dimer rises physiologically in pregnancy and is not validated to rule clot in or out.
Pregnancy-associated deep vein thrombosis is predominantly left-sided and proximal.
Absence of respiratory symptoms does not exclude clot but does make chest imaging the wrong first test.
explanation.pearls: A calf circumference difference of 2 cm or more measured 10 cm below the tibial tuberosity is one of the few bedside findings that meaningfully raises the probability of proximal deep vein thrombosis in pregnancy.

subtopic_detail: Interpreting a low D-dimer in suspected pregnancy deep vein thrombosis
stem:
A 34-year-old woman at 31 weeks presents to the emergency department with three days of right thigh and calf aching and a feeling that the leg is tight. She is a school teacher and spent last week largely off her feet after a minor ankle sprain on the other side.

The right leg is diffusely swollen to the groin with tenderness along the medial thigh; the ankle sprain on the left has settled. A D-dimer was collected at triage before you saw her and has returned at 0.42 mg/L fibrinogen equivalent units (reference less than 0.50). She has no bleeding history and takes no anticoagulant.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 94/min, BP 118/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius; foetal heart rate 148/min
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 116 g/L (110-140 in pregnancy); platelets 224 x10^9/L (150-400); creatinine 52 micromol/L (45-90)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Start therapeutic-dose enoxaparin now and arrange leg compression ultrasound the same day
options.rationale: Clinical probability is high with whole-leg swelling and recent immobility, and a D-dimer below the non-pregnant cut-off does not exclude clot in pregnancy; treat empirically and confirm with ultrasound, stopping treatment if imaging is negative. (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: Venous thromboembolism in pregnancy)
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: Venous thromboembolism in pregnancy
Australian Medicines Handbook: Enoxaparin

options.text: Reassure her that clot is excluded and review in a week if swelling persists
options.rationale: This uses a non-pregnant rule-out strategy in a population where it has never been validated; the standard pregnancy pathway is to image every symptomatic leg regardless of the D-dimer value. (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: Venous thromboembolism in pregnancy)
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: Venous thromboembolism in pregnancy

options.text: Repeat the D-dimer in 48 hours and arrange leg imaging only if raised
options.rationale: Serial D-dimer testing has no validated role in pregnancy and delays a test that could be done today; a rising level would in any case be expected from advancing gestation alone. (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: Venous thromboembolism in pregnancy)
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: Venous thromboembolism in pregnancy

options.text: Arrange a ventilation perfusion lung scan before any decision about anticoagulation is made
options.rationale: Chest imaging is for suspected pulmonary embolism and she has no respiratory symptoms; it also exposes her to radiation that adds nothing to a leg that needs an ultrasound. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guidelines: Venous thromboembolism (VTE) prophylaxis in pregnancy and the puerperium)
source_refs: Queensland Clinical Guidelines: Venous thromboembolism (VTE) prophylaxis in pregnancy and the puerperium

options.text: Commence prophylactic-dose enoxaparin and review her in the antenatal clinic in seven days
options.rationale: Prophylactic dosing is the wrong intensity when a clot is clinically suspected, and a week's delay allows propagation or embolisation; treatment dose plus prompt imaging is the safe pairing. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Enoxaparin)
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook: Enoxaparin

explanation.summary: D-dimer concentration rises steadily across normal pregnancy and is routinely above conventional cut-offs by the third trimester, which is why pregnancy-specific thresholds have never been prospectively validated for safe exclusion of clot. The practical consequence is that the D-dimer result should not change the imaging decision in a symptomatic pregnant woman, in either direction. Where clinical suspicion is high, empirical therapeutic low molecular weight heparin is started while imaging is arranged, because the risk of a few doses of heparin is far smaller than the risk of an untreated proximal clot. Anticoagulation is stopped if imaging is negative and suspicion resolves. In context, this question is about resisting a familiar non-pregnant algorithm rather than about knowing an unusual fact.
key_points: D-dimer is not validated to exclude venous thromboembolism at any stage of pregnancy.
Whole-leg swelling with recent immobility gives a high clinical probability that warrants empirical treatment.
Therapeutic low molecular weight heparin can be started and then stopped if imaging is negative.
Imaging should be same-day rather than deferred to outpatient review.
explanation.pearls: By the third trimester most healthy pregnant women have a D-dimer above 0.5 mg/L fibrinogen equivalent units, so the test loses the negative predictive value that makes it useful outside pregnancy.

subtopic_detail: Empirical anticoagulation while imaging is arranged for suspected pulmonary embolism
stem:
A 29-year-old woman at 33 weeks in her first pregnancy is brought in with sudden right-sided chest pain that catches when she breathes in, and breathlessness climbing a single flight of stairs. She has a body mass index of 33 and returned ten days ago from a flight home from Perth.

Her chest is clear on auscultation and her calves are soft and equal. An electrocardiogram shows sinus tachycardia only, and her chest radiograph is reported as normal. At her 28 week visit her oxygen saturation was recorded as 99 per cent on room air. She has had no fever and no cough.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 116/min, BP 108/66 mmHg, respiratory rate 26/min, SpO2 93% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius; foetal heart rate 152/min
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 112 g/L (110-140 in pregnancy); platelets 198 x10^9/L (150-400)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Withhold anticoagulation until definitive chest imaging has confirmed or excluded a clot
options.rationale: Delay is the commonest contributor to preventable maternal death from clot; with this probability the correct sequence is to treat first and let imaging decide whether treatment continues. (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: Venous thromboembolism in pregnancy)
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: Venous thromboembolism in pregnancy
Australian Institute of Health and Welfare: Maternal deaths in Australia

options.text: Give prophylactic-dose enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneously daily and arrange chest imaging tomorrow
options.rationale: Prophylactic dosing does not treat an established clot; it is the intensity used to prevent one, and pairing it with a day's delay compounds the error. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Enoxaparin)
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook: Enoxaparin

options.text: Give aspirin 300 mg orally now and arrange chest imaging within the next 24 hours
options.rationale: Antiplatelet therapy has no role in treating venous clot, which is fibrin-rich rather than platelet-rich; aspirin would neither prevent propagation nor reduce mortality here. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular - Venous thromboembolism)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular - Venous thromboembolism

options.text: Give therapeutic-dose enoxaparin now and arrange definitive chest imaging the same day
options.rationale: A fall in SpO2 with tachypnoea, tachycardia and a clear chest and normal radiograph makes clot the leading explanation; empirical treatment dose low molecular weight heparin started immediately is the intervention that changes mortality. (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: Venous thromboembolism in pregnancy)
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: Venous thromboembolism in pregnancy
Australian Medicines Handbook: Enoxaparin

options.text: Start an unfractionated heparin infusion titrated to the activated partial thromboplastin time ratio
options.rationale: Unfractionated heparin is reserved for haemodynamic instability, very high bleeding risk or severe renal impairment because its effect can be stopped quickly; she is stable, so low molecular weight heparin is preferred for its predictable dosing. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Enoxaparin)
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook: Enoxaparin

explanation.summary: Suspected pulmonary embolism in pregnancy is one of the few situations where treatment routinely precedes diagnosis. The rationale is asymmetric risk: a small number of doses of low molecular weight heparin in a woman who turns out not to have a clot causes very little harm, while several hours of untreated massive embolism can be fatal. Confirmatory imaging still matters, because a diagnosis of pregnancy-associated clot commits the woman to months of injections, alters management of the birth and shapes advice in future pregnancies, so it should never be left as a presumption. Unfractionated heparin is kept for the unstable woman or for those in whom rapid reversal may be required around imminent delivery. In context, the examinable judgement is the sequencing of treatment and imaging, not the choice of scan.
key_points: Start therapeutic low molecular weight heparin on clinical suspicion when the woman is stable and bleeding risk is low.
A normal chest radiograph and clear chest do not reduce the probability of pulmonary embolism.
Unfractionated heparin is preferred if haemodynamic instability, high bleeding risk or imminent delivery makes reversibility important.
Confirmatory imaging is still required because the diagnosis has long-term consequences.
explanation.pearls: A new drop in SpO2 from a documented earlier antenatal value is more useful than any single absolute reading, because healthy late pregnancy normally raises minute ventilation and keeps saturations at or above 97 per cent.

subtopic_detail: Choosing chest imaging for suspected pulmonary embolism when the chest radiograph is normal
stem:
A 26-year-old woman at 30 weeks is being assessed for two days of pleuritic left chest pain and exertional breathlessness. She has no family history of breast or ovarian cancer, and has already been started on therapeutic-dose enoxaparin.

Bilateral leg compression ultrasound showed no deep vein thrombosis. Her chest radiograph is reported as normal, with clear lung fields and a normal cardiac outline. She asks you what the next test will involve.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 104/min, BP 114/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 22/min, SpO2 95% on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius; foetal heart rate 146/min
data_table.Examination: Chest clear, calves soft and equal, no jugular venous distension
data_table.Investigations: Bilateral leg compression ultrasound negative; chest radiograph normal; creatinine 48 micromol/L (45-90)

lead_in: Which imaging investigation would you arrange next?

options.text: Computed tomography pulmonary angiogram with breast shielding and a reduced contrast volume
options.rationale: Computed tomography delivers a substantially higher radiation dose to maternal breast tissue, which is proliferating in pregnancy; it is the preferred study when the chest radiograph is abnormal, which is not the case here. (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: Venous thromboembolism in pregnancy)
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: Venous thromboembolism in pregnancy

options.text: Ventilation perfusion lung scan of the chest, beginning with the perfusion phase
options.rationale: With a normal chest radiograph the perfusion scan is highly likely to be diagnostic, and it spares the maternal breast the dose delivered by computed tomography; the ventilation phase can be omitted if perfusion is normal. (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: Venous thromboembolism in pregnancy)
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: Venous thromboembolism in pregnancy
Queensland Clinical Guidelines: Venous thromboembolism (VTE) prophylaxis in pregnancy and the puerperium

options.text: Repeat bilateral leg compression ultrasound in three days with interval clinical review
options.rationale: Repeat leg imaging is a reasonable strategy for suspected deep vein thrombosis with a negative first scan, but it cannot confirm or exclude clot in the pulmonary arteries when chest symptoms are the problem. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guidelines: Venous thromboembolism (VTE) prophylaxis in pregnancy and the puerperium)
source_refs: Queensland Clinical Guidelines: Venous thromboembolism (VTE) prophylaxis in pregnancy and the puerperium

options.text: Transthoracic echocardiography to look for right ventricular strain before any further imaging
options.rationale: Echocardiography is used to stratify severity in a haemodynamically unstable woman rather than to diagnose clot; a normal study in a stable woman does not exclude embolism. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular - Venous thromboembolism)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular - Venous thromboembolism

options.text: Plasma D-dimer to decide whether further chest imaging is justified at this gestation
options.rationale: D-dimer rises physiologically in pregnancy and cannot gate imaging decisions; using it here would either delay diagnosis or trigger a scan that was already indicated. (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: Venous thromboembolism in pregnancy)
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: Venous thromboembolism in pregnancy

explanation.summary: Both ventilation perfusion scanning and computed tomography pulmonary angiography deliver foetal radiation doses far below the roughly 100 milligray threshold associated with deterministic foetal harm, so the foetus is rarely the deciding factor. The real trade-off is that the perfusion scan gives a slightly higher foetal dose while computed tomography gives a much higher dose to maternal breast tissue, which is more radiosensitive in pregnancy and lactation. The chest radiograph is the tiebreaker: when it is normal, a perfusion scan is very likely to be interpretable, whereas parenchymal shadowing makes perfusion defects hard to attribute and pushes the choice toward computed tomography. Either study is preferable to leaving suspected embolism unresolved. In context, counselling should name both doses honestly rather than implying that one test is radiation-free.
key_points: Foetal dose from either study is well below the threshold for deterministic foetal effects.
Computed tomography gives a much higher maternal breast dose than a perfusion scan.
A normal chest radiograph favours ventilation perfusion scanning as the next test.
Leg ultrasound is done first when leg symptoms are present because a positive result avoids chest imaging altogether.
explanation.pearls: A perfusion-only first phase is often used in pregnancy, and if perfusion is normal the ventilation phase is omitted, roughly halving the dose of an already low-dose study.

subtopic_detail: Thromboprophylaxis during an antenatal admission with dehydration and immobility
stem:
A 23-year-old woman at 10 weeks in her first pregnancy has been admitted for the second time this month because she cannot keep fluids down. She has lost 5 kg since booking and has spent most of the past four days in bed on intravenous fluids and antiemetics.

Her booking weight was 72 kg and her body mass index at booking was 26. She has no personal or family history of clot and takes no other medicines. The nausea is improving on the current regimen and the team expects her to stay a further two days.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96/min, BP 104/62 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Dry mucous membranes, calves soft and equal, abdomen soft
data_table.Investigations: Urinary ketones 3+; sodium 133 mmol/L (135-145); potassium 3.3 mmol/L (3.5-5.2); creatinine 68 micromol/L (45-90); platelets 268 x10^9/L (150-400)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate addition to her inpatient management?

options.text: Aspirin 100 mg orally daily for the admission, then review at her next visit
options.rationale: Aspirin is used for pre-eclampsia prophylaxis, not venous thromboprophylaxis; it does not reduce venous clot risk meaningfully in this setting. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guidelines: Venous thromboembolism (VTE) prophylaxis in pregnancy and the puerperium)
source_refs: Queensland Clinical Guidelines: Venous thromboembolism (VTE) prophylaxis in pregnancy and the puerperium

options.text: Therapeutic-dose enoxaparin for the admission, then step down to a prophylactic dose on discharge
options.rationale: Treatment-dose anticoagulation is for a diagnosed clot; using it for prophylaxis exposes her to bleeding risk and complicates any procedure without added benefit. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Enoxaparin)
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook: Enoxaparin

options.text: No pharmacological prophylaxis, as clot risk is not appreciably raised in the first trimester
options.rationale: Clot risk is elevated from the first trimester onwards and hyperemesis with dehydration and immobility is a recognised trigger for admission-related prophylaxis. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guidelines: Venous thromboembolism (VTE) prophylaxis in pregnancy and the puerperium)
source_refs: Queensland Clinical Guidelines: Venous thromboembolism (VTE) prophylaxis in pregnancy and the puerperium

options.text: Graduated compression stockings alone for the admission, with early mobilisation encouraged each day
options.rationale: Mechanical measures are an adjunct and are reserved as the sole method when heparin is contraindicated; she has no contraindication, so omitting heparin under-treats her risk. (Source: Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care: Venous Thromboembolism Prevention Clinical Care Standard)
source_refs: Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care: Venous Thromboembolism Prevention Clinical Care Standard

options.text: Prophylactic-dose enoxaparin daily plus graduated compression stockings while she is an inpatient
options.rationale: Hyperemesis with dehydration and bed rest is an admission-level risk factor, and the standard response is prophylactic low molecular weight heparin for the duration of the admission with mechanical measures alongside. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guidelines: Venous thromboembolism (VTE) prophylaxis in pregnancy and the puerperium)
source_refs: Queensland Clinical Guidelines: Venous thromboembolism (VTE) prophylaxis in pregnancy and the puerperium
Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care: Venous Thromboembolism Prevention Clinical Care Standard

explanation.summary: Antenatal hospital admission is itself a venous thromboembolism risk factor, and hyperemesis gravidarum compounds it by adding haemoconcentration and immobility to the hypercoagulability of early pregnancy. Australian risk assessment tools require every pregnant inpatient to be scored on admission and rescored if her clinical state changes, with prophylaxis given for the duration of the admission unless bleeding risk forbids it. Prophylaxis is usually stopped at discharge once the woman is rehydrated and mobile, unless she has accumulated enough other risk factors to warrant continuing. Mechanical measures do not replace heparin in a woman with no contraindication. In context, the recurring examinable idea is that a risk assessment must be repeated at every admission rather than done once at booking.
key_points: Antenatal admission with dehydration and immobility triggers pharmacological prophylaxis.
Venous thromboembolism risk is raised from the first trimester, not only in late pregnancy.
Mechanical prophylaxis alone is for women in whom heparin is contraindicated.
Risk assessment is repeated at every admission and when clinical circumstances change.
explanation.pearls: Low molecular weight heparin does not cross the placenta, which is why it is the anticoagulant of choice throughout pregnancy while warfarin and the direct oral anticoagulants are avoided.

subtopic_detail: Prophylaxis plan after a previous surgery-provoked venous thromboembolism
stem:
A 31-year-old woman attends her booking visit at 9 weeks in her first pregnancy. Four years ago she had a calf deep vein thrombosis six days after a knee reconstruction, treated with three months of anticoagulation and no recurrence since.

Her body mass index is 24, she is a non-smoker and works as a physiotherapist on her feet all day. Thrombophilia testing was never done and no first-degree relative has had a clot. She asks what she needs during this pregnancy.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 76/min, BP 110/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Both calves soft and equal, no varicosities, healed knee surgical scar
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count and renal function within normal limits

lead_in: What thromboprophylaxis plan would you recommend?

options.text: Prophylactic-dose enoxaparin from today until six weeks after the birth of the baby
options.rationale: Antenatal prophylaxis from the first trimester is for a previous unprovoked or oestrogen-related event, or when other risk factors accumulate; her event had a clear transient surgical trigger. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guidelines: Venous thromboembolism (VTE) prophylaxis in pregnancy and the puerperium)
source_refs: Queensland Clinical Guidelines: Venous thromboembolism (VTE) prophylaxis in pregnancy and the puerperium

options.text: Prophylactic-dose enoxaparin from 28 weeks until the onset of labour, with nothing afterwards
options.rationale: This inverts the risk profile: the daily risk of clot is highest in the first weeks after birth, so omitting postnatal cover leaves the most dangerous period uncovered. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guidelines: Venous thromboembolism (VTE) prophylaxis in pregnancy and the puerperium)
source_refs: Queensland Clinical Guidelines: Venous thromboembolism (VTE) prophylaxis in pregnancy and the puerperium

options.text: No antenatal heparin, with prophylactic-dose enoxaparin for six weeks after the birth
options.rationale: A single previous event provoked by a transient major surgical trigger, with no thrombophilia and no other risk factors, does not by itself require antenatal heparin, but it does require six weeks of postnatal prophylaxis. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guidelines: Venous thromboembolism (VTE) prophylaxis in pregnancy and the puerperium)
source_refs: Queensland Clinical Guidelines: Venous thromboembolism (VTE) prophylaxis in pregnancy and the puerperium
Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care: Venous Thromboembolism Prevention Clinical Care Standard

options.text: No heparin at any stage, with graduated compression stockings worn throughout the pregnancy
options.rationale: Any previous venous thromboembolism raises the recurrence risk in the puerperium several-fold, so stockings alone under-treat her; heparin is required after the birth. (Source: Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care: Venous Thromboembolism Prevention Clinical Care Standard)
source_refs: Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care: Venous Thromboembolism Prevention Clinical Care Standard

options.text: Therapeutic-dose enoxaparin from today until six weeks after the birth of the baby
options.rationale: Treatment-intensity dosing across a whole pregnancy is reserved for women with a mechanical heart valve, a clot during this pregnancy, or very high-risk thrombophilia; she has none of these. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Enoxaparin)
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook: Enoxaparin

explanation.summary: Risk stratification for pregnancy thromboprophylaxis turns on whether a previous event was unprovoked, hormone-related, or provoked by a transient major trigger such as surgery or trauma. Unprovoked and oestrogen-related events carry a high recurrence risk in pregnancy and earn antenatal heparin from early in the first trimester. A single surgery-provoked event with no thrombophilia and no other current risk factors does not, but the postnatal period is a different matter: the relative risk of clot is at its peak in the first three weeks after birth and remains raised for about six weeks, so all women with any previous event receive postnatal prophylaxis. The plan must also be rescored if she develops new risk factors such as prolonged admission, pre-eclampsia or an emergency caesarean. In context, the distinction between provoked and unprovoked is the single most useful piece of history in the whole assessment.
key_points: A previous surgery-provoked event with no other risk factors does not mandate antenatal heparin.
Every woman with a previous venous thromboembolism receives six weeks of postnatal prophylaxis.
Unprovoked and oestrogen-related previous events do require antenatal prophylaxis from the first trimester.
The plan must be rescored if new antenatal or intrapartum risk factors appear.
explanation.pearls: The absolute risk of venous thromboembolism is roughly 20-fold higher in the first three weeks after birth than in the equivalent non-pregnant period, which is why postnatal cover is the part of the plan that is almost never omitted.

subtopic_detail: Timing of antenatal prophylaxis after an oestrogen-related previous clot
stem:
A 27-year-old woman comes to the early pregnancy clinic at 7 weeks having stopped her combined oral contraceptive four months ago. At the age of 22 she had an extensive femoral vein clot that began three months after starting that same contraceptive, and she completed six months of anticoagulation.

She is otherwise well with a body mass index of 23 and works as a graphic designer. No first-degree relative has had a clot, and thrombophilia testing after her event was negative. She is anxious about needle injections and asks whether anything can wait until later in pregnancy.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 80/min, BP 108/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Mild residual left thigh varicosities, both calves equal in circumference
data_table.Investigations: Platelets 246 x10^9/L (150-400); creatinine 56 micromol/L (45-90)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate plan for pharmacological thromboprophylaxis?

options.text: Start prophylactic-dose enoxaparin now and continue until six weeks after the birth
options.rationale: An event that began on combined hormonal contraception is oestrogen-related, and pregnancy is a sustained high-oestrogen state, so prophylaxis begins as soon as pregnancy is confirmed and runs through to six weeks postnatally. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guidelines: Venous thromboembolism (VTE) prophylaxis in pregnancy and the puerperium)
source_refs: Queensland Clinical Guidelines: Venous thromboembolism (VTE) prophylaxis in pregnancy and the puerperium
Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care: Venous Thromboembolism Prevention Clinical Care Standard

options.text: Start prophylactic-dose enoxaparin at 28 weeks and continue until six weeks after the birth
options.rationale: Deferring to the third trimester is the approach used when risk factors are intermediate and accumulating; an oestrogen-provoked previous event places her in the group that needs cover from the first trimester. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guidelines: Venous thromboembolism (VTE) prophylaxis in pregnancy and the puerperium)
source_refs: Queensland Clinical Guidelines: Venous thromboembolism (VTE) prophylaxis in pregnancy and the puerperium

options.text: Start prophylactic-dose enoxaparin at the onset of labour and continue for six weeks afterwards
options.rationale: Half of pregnancy-associated clots occur before labour, and heparin started in labour also collides with neuraxial analgesia timing; this leaves the entire antenatal period unprotected. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guidelines: Venous thromboembolism (VTE) prophylaxis in pregnancy and the puerperium)
source_refs: Queensland Clinical Guidelines: Venous thromboembolism (VTE) prophylaxis in pregnancy and the puerperium

options.text: Give low-dose aspirin now and add prophylactic-dose enoxaparin after the birth of the baby
options.rationale: Aspirin does not substitute for heparin in venous thromboprophylaxis; it is an antiplatelet agent with a role in pre-eclampsia prevention, not in preventing venous clot in a high-risk woman. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular - Venous thromboembolism)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular - Venous thromboembolism

options.text: Repeat the thrombophilia screen now and start prophylactic-dose enoxaparin only if it is positive
options.rationale: Management is driven by the clinical history rather than by laboratory thrombophilia status, and pregnancy itself alters protein S and activated protein C resistance results, making testing during pregnancy unreliable. (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: Venous thromboembolism in pregnancy)
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: Venous thromboembolism in pregnancy

explanation.summary: A previous clot that occurred while a woman was taking oestrogen-containing contraception is treated as hormone-provoked rather than as a transient provoked event, because the provoking exposure is repeated and amplified by pregnancy. Oestradiol concentrations in the third trimester are orders of magnitude above those produced by any contraceptive pill, and recurrence risk in these women approaches that of unprovoked events. Prophylaxis therefore starts when pregnancy is confirmed rather than at any gestational milestone, and continues for six weeks after the birth. A negative thrombophilia screen does not downgrade the plan, and repeating the screen during pregnancy produces results that are hard to interpret. In context, the lesson is that thrombophilia testing rarely changes obstetric management, whereas the circumstances of the index event almost always do.
key_points: Oestrogen-related previous clot is managed like an unprovoked event in pregnancy.
Prophylaxis starts at confirmation of pregnancy rather than at a set gestation.
Thrombophilia testing is unreliable during pregnancy and rarely changes management.
Aspirin is not a substitute for heparin in venous thromboprophylaxis.
explanation.pearls: Protein S concentration falls physiologically in pregnancy and free protein S can drop by 40 to 50 per cent by the third trimester, so a low result during pregnancy cannot be used to diagnose inherited deficiency.

subtopic_detail: Thromboprophylaxis when the postnatal platelet count is low
stem:
A 33-year-old woman is day 1 after an emergency caesarean at 34 weeks for severe pre-eclampsia. Her booking weight was 84 kg. She is receiving magnesium sulfate, is catheterised and has not yet been out of bed.

Her blood pressure is now controlled on oral labetalol and her liver enzymes are falling. The morning bloods show a platelet count of 58 x10^9/L, down from 96 x10^9/L before the birth, with no oozing from the wound or drip sites. The team asks you to write up her venous thromboembolism prevention.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92/min, BP 138/84 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Abdominal wound dry, uterus firm, calves soft and equal, no petechiae
data_table.Investigations: Platelets 58 x10^9/L (150-400); haemoglobin 94 g/L (115-165); alanine aminotransferase 74 U/L (5-30); creatinine 88 micromol/L (45-90); international normalised ratio 1.1 (0.8-1.2)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate venous thromboembolism prevention plan today?

options.text: Prophylactic-dose enoxaparin daily plus graduated compression stockings, starting this morning on the ward
options.rationale: Heparin is withheld while the platelet count sits below the accepted threshold and is still falling, because the bleeding risk after recent surgery outweighs the benefit until the count recovers. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guidelines: Venous thromboembolism (VTE) prophylaxis in pregnancy and the puerperium)
source_refs: Queensland Clinical Guidelines: Venous thromboembolism (VTE) prophylaxis in pregnancy and the puerperium

options.text: Prophylactic-dose enoxaparin at half the usual dose daily, with platelets rechecked tomorrow
options.rationale: Dose halving is not a recognised strategy for thrombocytopenia and there is no monitoring test to confirm safety; the decision is whether to give heparin at all, not at what fraction. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Enoxaparin)
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook: Enoxaparin

options.text: Transfuse one adult platelet unit, then commence prophylactic-dose enoxaparin later the same day
options.rationale: Platelet transfusion is for active bleeding or an invasive procedure rather than to enable prophylaxis, and pre-eclampsia-related thrombocytopenia usually recovers spontaneously within 48 to 72 hours of birth. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guidelines: Venous thromboembolism (VTE) prophylaxis in pregnancy and the puerperium)
source_refs: Queensland Clinical Guidelines: Venous thromboembolism (VTE) prophylaxis in pregnancy and the puerperium

options.text: Intermittent pneumatic compression alone, with the platelet count reassessed each day
options.rationale: She has several strong risk factors but a platelet count below the threshold at which heparin is considered safe, so mechanical prophylaxis covers her until the count recovers and heparin can be added. (Source: Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care: Venous Thromboembolism Prevention Clinical Care Standard)
source_refs: Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care: Venous Thromboembolism Prevention Clinical Care Standard
Queensland Clinical Guidelines: Venous thromboembolism (VTE) prophylaxis in pregnancy and the puerperium

options.text: No prophylaxis while she remains on magnesium sulfate and strict fluid restriction
options.rationale: Magnesium is not a reason to omit prophylaxis, and this woman has caesarean birth, pre-eclampsia, preterm birth and immobility stacked together; leaving her with nothing is the highest-risk option on the list. (Source: Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care: Venous Thromboembolism Prevention Clinical Care Standard)
source_refs: Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care: Venous Thromboembolism Prevention Clinical Care Standard

explanation.summary: Thromboprophylaxis decisions after birth are always a two-sided assessment: clot risk on one side and bleeding risk on the other. Severe pre-eclampsia sits awkwardly because it raises both, adding endothelial activation and caesarean birth to a falling platelet count. Australian guidance withholds low molecular weight heparin while platelets are below roughly 75 x10^9/L or where there is active bleeding or coagulopathy, and substitutes mechanical methods until the picture changes. Pre-eclamptic thrombocytopenia typically reaches its nadir within 24 to 48 hours of birth and then recovers, so the plan is explicitly a holding position with daily reassessment rather than a decision for the whole puerperium. In context, writing mechanical prophylaxis without a plan to review the platelets is as much an error as prescribing heparin too early.
key_points: Heparin prophylaxis is withheld when platelets are below about 75 x10^9/L or bleeding is active.
Mechanical prophylaxis covers the interval until heparin becomes safe.
Pre-eclampsia-related thrombocytopenia usually reaches its nadir within 48 hours of birth and then recovers.
Clot risk factors after severe pre-eclampsia accumulate rapidly and must be documented, not assumed.
explanation.pearls: Platelet count in pre-eclampsia typically begins to rise by the third postnatal day, so daily counts let heparin be started within 48 to 72 hours rather than being forgotten until discharge.

subtopic_detail: Thromboprophylaxis for lower limb immobilisation in the third trimester
stem:
A 30-year-old woman at 30 weeks in her second pregnancy attends the antenatal clinic two days after slipping at home. The orthopaedic team has applied a below-knee cast for an undisplaced fibular fracture and has asked her to remain non-weight-bearing on crutches for six weeks.

Her booking weight was 68 kg, she has no previous clot and no first-degree relative with clot. The pregnancy has otherwise been uncomplicated with normal growth on ultrasound last week. She has been sleeping downstairs on the couch since the injury because she cannot manage the stairs.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 84/min, BP 112/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 15/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius; foetal heart rate 144/min
data_table.Examination: Right below-knee cast in situ with warm toes and normal capillary refill, left calf soft
data_table.Investigations: Platelets 232 x10^9/L (150-400); haemoglobin 118 g/L (110-140 in pregnancy)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of her thrombotic risk?

options.text: Graduated compression stocking on the uncasted leg with advice to elevate both legs daily
options.rationale: Mechanical measures alone are for women in whom heparin is contraindicated; here they would leave a substantial and avoidable risk untreated for six weeks. (Source: Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care: Venous Thromboembolism Prevention Clinical Care Standard)
source_refs: Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care: Venous Thromboembolism Prevention Clinical Care Standard

options.text: Prophylactic-dose enoxaparin daily for as long as the cast and crutches are needed
options.rationale: Lower limb immobilisation in a cast during pregnancy stacks stasis on an already hypercoagulable state, and the standard response is prophylactic low molecular weight heparin for the duration of the immobility. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guidelines: Venous thromboembolism (VTE) prophylaxis in pregnancy and the puerperium)
source_refs: Queensland Clinical Guidelines: Venous thromboembolism (VTE) prophylaxis in pregnancy and the puerperium
Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care: Venous Thromboembolism Prevention Clinical Care Standard

options.text: Prophylactic-dose enoxaparin daily commencing at 36 weeks and continuing until the birth
options.rationale: Tying the start date to gestation ignores the actual trigger; the risk begins the day the cast was applied, not at an arbitrary later week. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guidelines: Venous thromboembolism (VTE) prophylaxis in pregnancy and the puerperium)
source_refs: Queensland Clinical Guidelines: Venous thromboembolism (VTE) prophylaxis in pregnancy and the puerperium

options.text: Serial compression ultrasound of the uncasted leg every two weeks until cast removal
options.rationale: Surveillance imaging detects clot after it has formed rather than preventing it, misses the casted limb, and is not a recognised substitute for prophylaxis. (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: Venous thromboembolism in pregnancy)
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: Venous thromboembolism in pregnancy

options.text: Aspirin 100 mg orally daily until she is weight-bearing again, then review in clinic
options.rationale: Aspirin is markedly less effective than heparin for venous clot prevention and is not the recommended agent for immobility-related risk in pregnancy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular - Venous thromboembolism)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular - Venous thromboembolism

explanation.summary: Pregnancy roughly quadruples the background risk of venous thromboembolism, and an added transient risk factor multiplies rather than adds to that baseline. Lower limb immobilisation in a cast is one of the strongest transient triggers available, which is why it scores heavily in every Australian maternity risk assessment tool. The prophylaxis is anchored to the duration of the trigger rather than to a gestational milestone, and the plan must be revisited at birth because caesarean or other intrapartum events may extend it into the puerperium. A woman who has needed antenatal heparin for immobility will usually also need postnatal cover for at least ten days. In context, most examinable thromboprophylaxis errors are errors of timing rather than of drug choice.
key_points: Lower limb immobilisation during pregnancy warrants prophylactic low molecular weight heparin.
Prophylaxis is timed to the duration of the transient risk factor, not to a gestation.
Mechanical measures alone are reserved for women with a contraindication to heparin.
The plan must be rescored around birth because new risk factors often extend it postnatally.
explanation.pearls: Pregnancy-associated clot risk is not uniform across the limbs: more than four in five deep vein thromboses in pregnancy occur in the left leg, so a symptomatic right leg still deserves the same imaging but is statistically less expected.

subtopic_detail: Fluctuant perineal swelling with fever after a repaired second-degree tear
stem:
A 24-year-old woman returns to the maternity assessment unit on day 5 after a normal vaginal birth with a repaired second-degree tear. She says the stitches have gone from sore to burning, she cannot sit down, and she noticed a bad smell on her pad this morning.

On examination the perineum is swollen and red over a 4 cm area lateral to the repair, with a tense fluctuant area at the centre and some of the suture line gaping. Her breasts are soft and her lochia is not offensive.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 104/min, BP 110/66 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 38.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 16.8 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0); C-reactive protein 92 mg/L (less than 5); haemoglobin 108 g/L (115-165)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Oral amoxicillin with clavulanate and warm salt baths, with clinic review in 48 hours
options.rationale: Antibiotics alone will not sterilise a collection under tension, and 48 hours of oral therapy risks extension into the ischiorectal fossa; drainage is required as well. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Obstetric and gynaecological infections)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Obstetric and gynaecological infections

options.text: Warm salt baths, simple analgesia and daily midwifery wound review until the swelling settles
options.rationale: Conservative wound care is appropriate for an inflamed but undrained wound without a collection; here it leaves an established collection and systemic upset untreated. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guidelines: Perineal care)
source_refs: Queensland Clinical Guidelines: Perineal care

options.text: Immediate secondary repair of the dehisced wound edges under regional anaesthesia in theatre
options.rationale: Resuturing infected tissue leads to repeat breakdown; the wound is left open to heal by secondary intention, with any delayed repair planned only after the infection has resolved. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guidelines: Perineal care)
source_refs: Queensland Clinical Guidelines: Perineal care

options.text: Magnetic resonance imaging of the pelvis and perineum before deciding on any intervention
options.rationale: Cross-sectional imaging is for suspected deep or complex extension when the examination findings are equivocal; a palpable fluctuant collection needs drainage rather than a scan. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guidelines: Perineal care)
source_refs: Queensland Clinical Guidelines: Perineal care

options.text: Incision and drainage in theatre with wound swabs taken and intravenous antibiotics
options.rationale: A fluctuant collection with systemic features requires source control; drainage plus culture-directed intravenous antibiotics treats both the collection and the surrounding tissue infection. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Obstetric and gynaecological infections)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Obstetric and gynaecological infections
Queensland Clinical Guidelines: Perineal care

explanation.summary: Perineal wound infection complicates a small but meaningful proportion of vaginal births, and it is under-recognised because early wound pain is expected after any repair. The features that separate infection from normal healing are pain that worsens rather than improves after day 3, purulent or malodorous discharge, wound gaping and fever. Where a collection is present the governing principle is the same as anywhere else in surgery: no amount of antibiotic substitutes for drainage. Infected perineal wounds are then managed open, with delayed repair considered only once granulation is established, because resuturing infected tissue reliably breaks down again. In context, a woman sent home on oral antibiotics without drainage is the typical path to readmission with a much larger problem.
key_points: Perineal pain that worsens after day 3 with fever suggests wound infection rather than normal healing.
A fluctuant collection requires incision and drainage regardless of antibiotic cover.
Infected perineal wounds heal by secondary intention; immediate resuturing fails.
Take wound swabs at drainage so that antibiotic therapy can be narrowed.
explanation.pearls: Rapidly spreading erythema with pain disproportionate to the findings and systemic collapse should prompt consideration of necrotising infection, which needs urgent surgical exploration rather than simple drainage.

subtopic_detail: Spreading redness around a caesarean wound without a collection
stem:
A 29-year-old woman is seen on day 6 after an elective caesarean because the skin around her scar has become red and sore over the past day. She is eating normally, feeding her baby and walking to the shops.

The uterus is well contracted and non-tender and her lochia is light. Careful palpation of the wound finds it warm and tender but with no fluctuance and no discharge. She has needed nothing stronger than paracetamol for the pain.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88/min, BP 116/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 37.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Erythema extending 4 cm above the incision, warm and tender to touch
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 12.4 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0); C-reactive protein 46 mg/L (less than 5); bedside wound ultrasound shows no collection

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Oral flucloxacillin 500 mg four times daily, marking the erythema border for review
options.rationale: Cellulitis around a caesarean wound in a systemically well woman is treated with an oral antistaphylococcal agent, and marking the margin gives an objective measure of response at review. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Skin and soft tissue infections)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Skin and soft tissue infections
Australian Medicines Handbook: Flucloxacillin

options.text: Intravenous cefazolin 2 g eight-hourly with admission for close observation of the wound margin
options.rationale: Intravenous therapy and admission are for systemic sepsis, failure of oral treatment or rapidly advancing erythema; she is afebrile and eating, so oral therapy with early review is proportionate. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Skin and soft tissue infections)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Skin and soft tissue infections

options.text: Open the lower third of the wound on the ward, with oral antibiotics afterwards
options.rationale: Opening a wound is the treatment for a collection or necrotic tissue; with no fluctuance and no collection on ultrasound this converts an intact wound into an open one for no benefit. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Obstetric and gynaecological infections)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Obstetric and gynaecological infections

options.text: Oral metronidazole 400 mg twice daily with simple analgesia and review in the clinic next week
options.rationale: Metronidazole covers anaerobes and has no useful activity against the staphylococci and streptococci that cause surgical site cellulitis; a week is also too long to wait for reassessment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Skin and soft tissue infections)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Skin and soft tissue infections

options.text: Simple analgesia and wound observation alone, with advice to return if she develops any fever
options.rationale: Established cellulitis with a raised C-reactive protein does not resolve without antibiotics, and waiting for fever delays treatment until the infection is already systemic. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Skin and soft tissue infections)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Skin and soft tissue infections

explanation.summary: Surgical site infection follows around two to five per cent of caesarean births in Australia and is one of the commonest reasons for postnatal readmission. Most of it is superficial incisional infection caused by skin flora, chiefly Staphylococcus aureus and beta-haemolytic streptococci, which responds to an oral antistaphylococcal penicillin when the woman is systemically well and there is no collection. The two decisions that matter are whether a collection needs drainage and whether the infection is systemic enough to need intravenous therapy and admission. Marking the erythema margin is a simple way of making the follow-up decision objective rather than impressionistic. In context, deep and organ-space infection, including endometritis, must always be looked for at the same visit, since the two often coexist after caesarean.
key_points: Superficial caesarean wound cellulitis in a well woman is treated orally with an antistaphylococcal agent.
Absence of fluctuance and a negative wound ultrasound argue against drainage.
Mark the erythema border so that progression can be judged objectively at review.
Always examine the uterus and lochia, since endometritis can coexist with wound infection.
explanation.pearls: Flucloxacillin 500 mg orally four times daily on an empty stomach is the standard Australian choice for staphylococcal wound cellulitis, and it is compatible with breastfeeding.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Skin and soft tissue infections
Australian Medicines Handbook: Flucloxacillin
Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Obstetric and gynaecological infections

subtopic_detail: Breast infection with systemic features and haemodynamic change
stem:
A 32-year-old woman presents at 3 weeks postnatal with a painful right breast that began yesterday. Overnight she had two episodes of shaking that woke her partner, and this morning she felt faint standing up to feed.

The upper outer quadrant of the right breast is red, firm and very tender over an 8 cm wedge with no discrete lump and no fluctuance. She has vomited twice and has not been able to keep fluids down since waking. Her baby is feeding well from the left breast and has no thrush.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 124/min, BP 92/54 mmHg, respiratory rate 24/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 39.2 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 19.2 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0); C-reactive protein 164 mg/L (less than 5); lactate 3.1 mmol/L (less than 2.0); creatinine 96 micromol/L (45-90)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Oral dicloxacillin 500 mg four times daily with feeding continued and review tomorrow
options.rationale: Oral therapy is appropriate for mastitis in a systemically well woman; with hypotension, tachycardia and a raised lactate she also cannot reliably absorb oral antibiotics after vomiting. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Mastitis)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Mastitis

options.text: Cold packs, effective milk removal and ibuprofen, with antibiotics only if unimproved
options.rationale: Conservative measures are first-line for an inflammatory breast without systemic infection; delaying antibiotics in a woman with these observations risks progression to septic shock. (Source: Australian Breastfeeding Association: Mastitis)
source_refs: Australian Breastfeeding Association: Mastitis

options.text: Admit for intravenous flucloxacillin with fluid resuscitation and continued milk removal
options.rationale: Systemic features with hypotension and a raised lactate meet criteria for sepsis, requiring admission, intravenous antistaphylococcal therapy, resuscitation and ongoing drainage of the affected breast. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Mastitis)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Mastitis
Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care: Sepsis Clinical Care Standard

options.text: Urgent breast ultrasound with needle aspiration of the affected quadrant before antibiotics
options.rationale: Imaging is indicated when a collection is suspected after failed therapy or when a discrete lump is present, but no drainable focus is palpable and delaying antibiotics in sepsis worsens outcome. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Mastitis)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Mastitis

options.text: Stop feeding from the right breast and give oral cefalexin 500 mg six-hourly
options.rationale: Stopping drainage of an infected breast causes stasis and worsens the infection; feeding or expressing from the affected side is part of treatment and is safe for the baby. (Source: Australian Breastfeeding Association: Mastitis)
source_refs: Australian Breastfeeding Association: Mastitis

explanation.summary: Lactational mastitis is common and usually manageable in the community, but a small proportion of women progress to bacteraemia and septic shock, and Staphylococcus aureus is the usual organism. The decision point is not the appearance of the breast but the systemic picture: rigors, hypotension, tachycardia, altered mental state or a raised lactate all move the woman from oral to intravenous therapy and from home to hospital. Milk removal continues throughout, because stasis in an infected lobule is what allowed the infection to establish, and abrupt cessation increases the risk of abscess. Ultrasound is added when a collection is suspected or when there is no improvement after 48 hours of appropriate therapy. In context, sepsis from any source remains a leading direct cause of maternal death in Australia, and the breast is an easily overlooked source.
key_points: Rigors, hypotension and raised lactate move mastitis from oral to intravenous management.
Continue milk removal from the affected breast throughout treatment.
Staphylococcus aureus is the usual pathogen, so cover must be antistaphylococcal.
Reserve ultrasound for a suspected collection or failure to improve after 48 hours.
explanation.pearls: A nipple fissure is the usual portal of entry for Staphylococcus aureus in lactational mastitis, so correcting attachment is as much a part of treatment as the antibiotic.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Mastitis

subtopic_detail: Duration of treatment after a pulmonary embolism diagnosed in pregnancy
stem:
A 35-year-old woman had a segmental pulmonary embolism confirmed at 29 weeks and has been on therapeutic-dose enoxaparin since. She is now 36 weeks, her symptoms have resolved and the pregnancy is otherwise uncomplicated.

She has no previous clot, her thrombophilia status is unknown and she plans to breastfeed. At today's visit she asks how long she will need to keep taking injections after the baby is born, and whether she can change to tablets.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 82/min, BP 114/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius; foetal heart rate 140/min
data_table.Examination: Chest clear, calves soft and equal, symphysis fundal height appropriate for dates
data_table.Investigations: Platelets 208 x10^9/L (150-400); creatinine 60 micromol/L (45-90); haemoglobin 114 g/L (110-140 in pregnancy)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice about the duration and choice of her anticoagulation?

options.text: Stop anticoagulation once she has given birth, as the provoking factor will have resolved
options.rationale: The puerperium carries the highest daily risk of recurrence of the whole pregnancy, so stopping at birth removes cover exactly when it is most needed. (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: Venous thromboembolism in pregnancy)
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: Venous thromboembolism in pregnancy

options.text: Continue treatment dose until birth, then reduce to a prophylactic dose for ten days only
options.rationale: Ten days of prophylactic dosing is the plan for risk-factor-based prevention, not for a clot that has actually occurred and needs a minimum total treatment course. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guidelines: Venous thromboembolism (VTE) prophylaxis in pregnancy and the puerperium)
source_refs: Queensland Clinical Guidelines: Venous thromboembolism (VTE) prophylaxis in pregnancy and the puerperium

options.text: Change to rivaroxaban now so that she is established on tablets before she begins feeding
options.rationale: Direct oral anticoagulants cross the placenta and are not recommended in pregnancy, and there are insufficient data to support their use while breastfeeding. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Enoxaparin)
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook: Enoxaparin

options.text: Continue treatment dose until birth, then change to aspirin 100 mg daily for three months
options.rationale: Aspirin is far less effective than anticoagulation for preventing recurrent venous clot and does not count toward a treatment course. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular - Venous thromboembolism)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular - Venous thromboembolism

options.text: Continue treatment dose for at least six weeks postnatally and three months in total
options.rationale: Pregnancy-associated venous thromboembolism is treated for a minimum of three months overall and for at least six weeks after birth, whichever is longer, and enoxaparin or warfarin may be used while breastfeeding. (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: Venous thromboembolism in pregnancy)
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: Venous thromboembolism in pregnancy
Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular - Venous thromboembolism

explanation.summary: Treatment of a clot diagnosed in pregnancy is governed by two overlapping rules: a minimum total treatment duration of three months, as for any provoked venous thromboembolism, and a minimum of six weeks of postnatal cover, because the puerperium is the highest-risk window. A clot diagnosed late in pregnancy is therefore treated well beyond birth, while one diagnosed in the first trimester may finish its three months before the third trimester and then be continued at either treatment or prophylactic intensity to the end of the puerperium. Low molecular weight heparin remains the agent of choice antenatally because it does not cross the placenta, and both heparin and warfarin are compatible with breastfeeding. The direct oral anticoagulants are avoided in pregnancy and lactation. In context, this is a counselling question a Year 4 student will be asked on the ward round, and the two overlapping minimums are what must be remembered.
key_points: Minimum three months of treatment in total and at least six weeks postnatally, whichever is longer.
Low molecular weight heparin does not cross the placenta and is the antenatal agent of choice.
Enoxaparin and warfarin are both compatible with breastfeeding.
Direct oral anticoagulants are avoided in pregnancy and are not recommended during lactation.
explanation.pearls: Warfarin is safe in breastfeeding because negligible amounts enter breast milk, which is why it is a reasonable postnatal step-down from enoxaparin when weeks of further treatment are needed.

subtopic_detail: Large breast collection with overlying skin compromise
stem:
A 30-year-old woman is reviewed at 5 weeks postnatal, having completed seven days of oral flucloxacillin for a right breast infection. The pain settled briefly and then returned, and she now describes the breast as feeling tight and heavy.

Examination shows a 5 cm firm tender mass in the lower outer quadrant with a shiny, thinned and dusky 2 cm patch of overlying skin that blanches poorly. Ultrasound reports a 52 mm multiloculated collection with thick internal debris extending to within 2 mm of the skin surface. She remains afebrile and is feeding from the left breast.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92/min, BP 112/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 37.2 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 13.6 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0); C-reactive protein 58 mg/L (less than 5)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of the collection?

options.text: Repeat ultrasound-guided needle aspiration every 48 hours with a further week of oral antibiotics
options.rationale: Needle aspiration works well for smaller unilocular collections with healthy overlying skin, but multiloculated collections with thin necrotic skin recur and eventually rupture spontaneously. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Mastitis)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Mastitis

options.text: Surgical incision and drainage with division of loculi and tissue sent for culture
options.rationale: Multiloculated collections above about 5 cm with compromised overlying skin require formal drainage with division of septations, and tissue culture guides further antibiotic choice. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Mastitis)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Mastitis
Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Skin and soft tissue infections

options.text: Change to oral trimethoprim with sulfamethoxazole for a further ten days and review in clinic
options.rationale: Changing the antibiotic addresses the possibility of resistant organisms but leaves an established collection undrained, which is the reason the first course failed. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Mastitis)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Mastitis

options.text: Stop breastfeeding entirely and use cabergoline to suppress lactation before any further treatment
options.rationale: Suppressing lactation is not required and removes ongoing drainage of the breast; feeding or expressing may continue, including from the affected side once drainage is established. (Source: Australian Breastfeeding Association: Mastitis)
source_refs: Australian Breastfeeding Association: Mastitis

options.text: Urgent triple assessment with core biopsy and mammography before any drainage is undertaken
options.rationale: Triple assessment is warranted when a breast mass persists after treatment or when inflammatory malignancy is suspected; here the ultrasound has already defined a drainable collection needing source control. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Mastitis)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Mastitis

explanation.summary: Around one in twenty women with lactational mastitis develops an abscess, most often after delayed or inadequate antibiotic treatment or after milk removal was stopped. Ultrasound-guided needle aspiration, repeated as required and combined with antibiotics, is the preferred first approach for most collections because it preserves the breast and allows continued feeding. Formal surgical drainage is reserved for large multiloculated collections, for those where the overlying skin is thinned or necrotic, and for failure of aspiration. Breastfeeding continues throughout in either approach, since milk stasis promotes recurrence. In context, any breast mass that does not resolve completely after treatment needs triple assessment, because inflammatory breast cancer can present in a lactating woman and mimic infection.
key_points: Ultrasound-guided aspiration is first-line for most lactational breast abscesses.
Formal incision and drainage is indicated for large multiloculated collections or compromised skin.
Continue milk removal from the affected breast during and after drainage.
A mass that persists after adequate treatment requires triple assessment.
explanation.pearls: Send drained material for culture: methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus is an increasing cause of breast abscess in the community and will not respond to flucloxacillin.

subtopic_detail: Maternal fever in labour with prolonged rupture of membranes
stem:
A 27-year-old woman at 39 weeks is in labour on the birth suite. Her membranes ruptured 22 hours ago and she has had six vaginal examinations since admission. She is 6 cm dilated with regular contractions and an epidural in situ.

Over the past hour her temperature has risen from 37.1 to 38.5 degrees Celsius and her pulse has climbed to 118 per minute. The cardiotocograph shows a baseline of 172 beats per minute with reduced variability and no decelerations. Her uterus is tender between contractions and the liquor draining onto the pad has an offensive smell.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118/min, BP 108/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 22/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 38.5 degrees Celsius; foetal heart rate baseline 172/min
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 21.4 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0); C-reactive protein 118 mg/L (less than 5); lactate 1.8 mmol/L (less than 2.0)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Intravenous paracetamol and cooling measures, with reassessment of the cardiotocograph in one hour
options.rationale: Treating the temperature without treating its cause leaves an intrauterine infection untreated and may mask the deterioration that would otherwise prompt escalation. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guidelines: Sepsis in pregnancy and the puerperium)
source_refs: Queensland Clinical Guidelines: Sepsis in pregnancy and the puerperium

options.text: Intravenous benzylpenicillin alone as group B streptococcal prophylaxis, continuing expectant care
options.rationale: Single-agent intrapartum prophylaxis is for colonisation without infection; established intrauterine infection needs broad-spectrum cover including gram-negative and anaerobic organisms. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Obstetric and gynaecological infections)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Obstetric and gynaecological infections

options.text: Immediate caesarean section under general anaesthesia irrespective of her progress in labour
options.rationale: Caesarean in the presence of intrauterine infection carries added wound and endometritis risk and is not automatic; it is used if labour fails to progress or the foetal condition deteriorates. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guidelines: Sepsis in pregnancy and the puerperium)
source_refs: Queensland Clinical Guidelines: Sepsis in pregnancy and the puerperium

options.text: Blood cultures then broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics, with a plan to expedite birth
options.rationale: Intrauterine infection in labour requires cultures, prompt broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics and delivery of the uterine contents, since the uterus is the source and antibiotics alone will not clear it. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Obstetric and gynaecological infections)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Obstetric and gynaecological infections
Queensland Clinical Guidelines: Sepsis in pregnancy and the puerperium

options.text: Oral amoxicillin with clavulanate and continued hourly observations until the second stage begins
options.rationale: Oral therapy gives unreliable absorption and inadequate tissue concentrations in a septic labouring woman, and delays effective treatment of both mother and baby. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Obstetric and gynaecological infections)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Obstetric and gynaecological infections

explanation.summary: Intrauterine infection in labour threatens two patients at once. For the mother it can progress to bacteraemia, septic shock and postpartum haemorrhage from a poorly contracting infected uterus; for the baby it raises the risk of early onset neonatal sepsis and, at preterm gestations, of neurological injury. Prolonged rupture of membranes and repeated vaginal examinations are the two commonest antecedents. Management is broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics started promptly after cultures, continuous foetal monitoring, and birth without undue delay, with the mode of birth decided on obstetric grounds rather than by the infection itself. The paediatric team must be told before the birth so the baby can be assessed and treated. In context, foetal tachycardia above 160 beats per minute in the setting of maternal fever should be read as a sign of infection rather than as a separate problem.
key_points: Prolonged membrane rupture and repeated vaginal examinations are the main risk factors.
Take blood cultures then give broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics without waiting for results.
Expedite birth, with mode of birth decided on obstetric grounds.
Alert the paediatric team before the birth because of the risk of early onset neonatal sepsis.
explanation.pearls: Persistent foetal tachycardia with reduced variability alongside maternal fever is the cardiotocograph signature of intrauterine infection and should not be attributed to the epidural.
