subtopic_detail: Chest imaging choice when the radiograph is abnormal and breast dose matters
stem:
A 34-year-old woman at 32 weeks has had four days of right-sided pleuritic chest pain and breathlessness on minimal exertion, with a dry cough. Bilateral leg compression ultrasound was negative this morning and she has been started on therapeutic-dose enoxaparin.

Her mother and her older sister were both diagnosed with breast cancer in their forties, and she has read that chest scans deliver radiation to the breast. Her chest radiograph shows a wedge-shaped opacity in the right lower zone with a small pleural effusion. She has remained afebrile with a normal white cell count and a C-reactive protein of 6 mg/L.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 108/min, BP 116/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 24/min, SpO2 94% on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius; foetal heart rate 148/min
data_table.Examination: Reduced air entry at the right base, calves soft and equal, no jugular venous distension
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 9.1 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0); C-reactive protein 6 mg/L (less than 5); creatinine 54 micromol/L (45-90)

lead_in: Which imaging investigation would you arrange next?

options.text: Computed tomography pulmonary angiogram, counselling her about the dose to breast tissue
options.rationale: Parenchymal shadowing makes perfusion defects impossible to attribute, so a scan that images the pulmonary arteries directly is required; the higher breast dose is a genuine cost to disclose, not a reason to accept a non-diagnostic study. (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: Venous thromboembolism in pregnancy)
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: Venous thromboembolism in pregnancy

options.text: Ventilation perfusion lung scan, since it delivers a much lower dose to breast tissue
options.rationale: The lower breast dose is real, but a perfusion defect matching a radiographic opacity is indeterminate, so this study is likely to leave the question unanswered and require a second scan anyway. (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: Venous thromboembolism in pregnancy)
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: Venous thromboembolism in pregnancy

options.text: Repeat bilateral leg compression ultrasound in three days, continuing the current treatment
options.rationale: Serial leg imaging is a reasonable strategy when leg symptoms are the problem, but here it cannot explain hypoxia and a radiographic abnormality, and leaves her on indefinite empirical treatment. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guidelines: Venous thromboembolism (VTE) prophylaxis in pregnancy and the puerperium)
source_refs: Queensland Clinical Guidelines: Venous thromboembolism (VTE) prophylaxis in pregnancy and the puerperium

options.text: Empirical antibiotics with a repeat chest radiograph in 48 hours to assess for resolution
options.rationale: A normal white cell count, normal C-reactive protein and absence of fever argue strongly against pneumonia, and the wedge-shaped peripheral opacity with effusion is more consistent with infarction. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular - Venous thromboembolism)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular - Venous thromboembolism

options.text: Magnetic resonance pulmonary angiography, avoiding ionising radiation to the breast and foetus
options.rationale: Magnetic resonance angiography of the pulmonary arteries has a high rate of technically inadequate studies and is not recommended as the pathway test for suspected pulmonary embolism in pregnancy. (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: Venous thromboembolism in pregnancy)
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: Venous thromboembolism in pregnancy

explanation.summary: The choice between perfusion scanning and computed tomography in pregnancy is usually decided by the chest radiograph rather than by dose alone. A normal radiograph favours perfusion scanning, which is highly likely to be diagnostic and spares maternal breast tissue; an abnormal radiograph makes perfusion defects uninterpretable, since parenchymal disease produces matched defects, and pushes the choice toward direct angiography. Family history of breast cancer is a legitimate consideration and belongs in the conversation with the woman, but it cannot justify choosing a test that will probably need repeating. Foetal dose from either modality is well under the threshold associated with deterministic foetal effects, and diagnostic uncertainty carries its own substantial risk. In context, the honest counselling position is that both studies carry a small radiation cost and that an indeterminate scan is itself a harm.
key_points: An abnormal chest radiograph makes ventilation perfusion scanning likely to be indeterminate.
Computed tomography delivers a higher maternal breast dose but a lower foetal dose than perfusion scanning.
Normal inflammatory markers and absence of fever argue against pneumonia as the explanation.
Magnetic resonance pulmonary angiography is not an accepted alternative pathway test in pregnancy.
explanation.pearls: A peripheral wedge-shaped opacity abutting the pleura with a small effusion, in an afebrile woman with normal inflammatory markers, is the radiographic pattern of pulmonary infarction rather than of pneumonia.

subtopic_detail: Neuraxial block timing after a prophylactic dose of low molecular weight heparin
stem:
A 31-year-old woman at 39 weeks is on the morning list for an elective caesarean for breech presentation. She has been taking prophylactic-dose enoxaparin since the first trimester after a previous clot, and her last injection was at 10 pm last night.

It is now 6 am and she is first on the list. Her platelet count is 214 x10^9/L, her creatinine is 58 micromol/L and she takes no other anticoagulant or antiplatelet medicine. The anaesthetic registrar asks for your view before the woman is brought around.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 80/min, BP 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 15/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius; foetal heart rate 142/min
data_table.Examination: Breech presentation confirmed, uterus soft, no contractions, back examination unremarkable
data_table.Investigations: Platelets 214 x10^9/L (150-400); creatinine 58 micromol/L (45-90); international normalised ratio 1.0 (0.8-1.2)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate plan for her anaesthesia?

options.text: Proceed with a spinal block now, since eight hours is adequate after a prophylactic dose
options.rationale: Eight hours falls short of the accepted interval after a prophylactic dose, and the consequence of getting it wrong is spinal haematoma with permanent neurological injury. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guidelines: Venous thromboembolism (VTE) prophylaxis in pregnancy and the puerperium)
source_refs: Queensland Clinical Guidelines: Venous thromboembolism (VTE) prophylaxis in pregnancy and the puerperium

options.text: Proceed now under general anaesthesia so that the operating list is not delayed today
options.rationale: General anaesthesia is the correct fallback for a genuinely urgent caesarean inside the heparin window, but it carries higher airway and aspiration risk and is not justified to protect a list for an elective case. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guidelines: Venous thromboembolism (VTE) prophylaxis in pregnancy and the puerperium)
source_refs: Queensland Clinical Guidelines: Venous thromboembolism (VTE) prophylaxis in pregnancy and the puerperium

options.text: Delay the block until at least 12 hours have passed since her last prophylactic dose
options.rationale: The accepted interval between a prophylactic dose of low molecular weight heparin and a neuraxial block is 12 hours, so waiting a further few hours allows a spinal safely for an elective procedure. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guidelines: Venous thromboembolism (VTE) prophylaxis in pregnancy and the puerperium)
source_refs: Queensland Clinical Guidelines: Venous thromboembolism (VTE) prophylaxis in pregnancy and the puerperium
Australian Medicines Handbook: Enoxaparin

options.text: Give intravenous protamine sulfate to reverse the heparin and perform the spinal in one hour
options.rationale: Protamine only partially reverses low molecular weight heparin and is reserved for significant bleeding; it is not used to shorten the interval before a planned neuraxial block. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Enoxaparin)
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook: Enoxaparin

options.text: Measure an anti-Xa concentration now and perform the spinal if the level is below 0.2 IU/mL
options.rationale: Anti-Xa monitoring has no validated threshold for the safety of neuraxial puncture and is not available quickly enough to guide this decision; the timed interval remains the standard. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Enoxaparin)
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook: Enoxaparin

explanation.summary: Spinal and epidural haematoma is rare but catastrophic, and the whole of obstetric anticoagulation planning around birth is built to avoid it. The intervals used in Australian maternity units are 12 hours between a prophylactic dose of low molecular weight heparin and a neuraxial block or catheter removal, and 24 hours after a treatment dose. After the block or after catheter removal, the next heparin dose is withheld for at least 4 hours. Women on antenatal heparin are therefore usually converted to a planned birth so these windows can be engineered rather than improvised, and are told to omit the dose once contractions begin or bleeding starts. In context, the commonest real-world failure is not ignorance of the interval but failure to document the exact time of the last dose.
key_points: Twelve hours between a prophylactic dose and neuraxial block or catheter removal.
Twenty-four hours is required after a treatment dose.
The next heparin dose is delayed at least 4 hours after the block or catheter removal.
General anaesthesia is the alternative when the caesarean cannot wait for the interval.
explanation.pearls: Document the clock time of the last enoxaparin dose in the notes rather than the date alone, since the entire neuraxial plan depends on an interval measured in hours.

subtopic_detail: Managing treatment-dose heparin around a planned birth
stem:
A 33-year-old woman at 37 weeks has been on treatment-dose enoxaparin twice daily since a femoral vein clot was diagnosed at 24 weeks. An induction of labour has been booked for 39 weeks and she is well, with no bleeding and a normally grown baby.

She asks whether she will be able to have an epidural, saying that she managed poorly without one in her first labour. Her last dose today was at 8 am and she has been shown how to self-inject. The plan for her birth is being written in the antenatal clinic today.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 84/min, BP 112/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 15/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius; foetal heart rate 146/min
data_table.Examination: Cephalic presentation, symphysis fundal height 37 cm, calves soft and equal
data_table.Investigations: Platelets 236 x10^9/L (150-400); haemoglobin 116 g/L (110-140 in pregnancy); creatinine 55 micromol/L (45-90)

lead_in: What plan for her anticoagulation around the birth would you document today?

options.text: Continue both daily doses up to admission, accepting that epidural analgesia may be unavailable
options.rationale: Continuing treatment-dose heparin into the induction closes the neuraxial window unnecessarily for a planned birth, and also raises bleeding risk at delivery. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guidelines: Venous thromboembolism (VTE) prophylaxis in pregnancy and the puerperium)
source_refs: Queensland Clinical Guidelines: Venous thromboembolism (VTE) prophylaxis in pregnancy and the puerperium

options.text: Omit the treatment dose for 24 hours before the planned induction, then reassess on admission
options.rationale: A 24-hour interval after a treatment dose is what makes neuraxial analgesia safe, and planning the omission around a booked induction is exactly why induction is offered to anticoagulated women. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guidelines: Venous thromboembolism (VTE) prophylaxis in pregnancy and the puerperium)
source_refs: Queensland Clinical Guidelines: Venous thromboembolism (VTE) prophylaxis in pregnancy and the puerperium
Australian Medicines Handbook: Enoxaparin

options.text: Omit the treatment dose for 12 hours before the planned induction, then reassess on admission
options.rationale: Twelve hours is the interval that applies after a prophylactic dose; a treatment dose leaves substantially more residual anti-Xa activity and requires double that interval. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Enoxaparin)
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook: Enoxaparin

options.text: Change to warfarin at 38 weeks so that her anticoagulation can be reversed at the birth
options.rationale: Warfarin crosses the placenta and would anticoagulate the foetus during labour, creating a risk of neonatal intracranial haemorrhage; it is avoided near term. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Enoxaparin)
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook: Enoxaparin

options.text: Stop anticoagulation entirely from 38 weeks and restart at a prophylactic dose after the birth
options.rationale: Stopping treatment altogether in the last weeks leaves a recent clot unprotected in the highest-risk period, and stepping down to prophylaxis does not complete the treatment course. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular - Venous thromboembolism)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular - Venous thromboembolism

explanation.summary: Anticoagulated women are usually offered a planned birth precisely so that the heparin-free window can be engineered rather than left to chance. The two intervals that shape every plan are 12 hours after a prophylactic dose and 24 hours after a treatment dose before a neuraxial block or catheter removal, with the next dose delayed at least 4 hours afterwards. Women on treatment-dose heparin are also advised to omit their dose and contact the unit at the onset of contractions or bleeding, because spontaneous labour can otherwise arrive inside the window. Some units convert high-risk women to twice-daily dosing or to unfractionated heparin close to term because its shorter half-life gives more flexibility. In context, the plan needs a named start time for omission, not just a general instruction to stop before birth.
key_points: Twenty-four hours between a treatment dose and neuraxial block or catheter removal.
Planned induction or caesarean allows the heparin-free window to be scheduled.
Advise omission of the dose at the onset of labour or any bleeding.
Warfarin near term risks neonatal intracranial haemorrhage and is avoided.
explanation.pearls: Unfractionated heparin has a half-life of around 60 to 90 minutes and can be stopped 4 to 6 hours before a block, which is why some units switch very high-risk women to an infusion in the final week.

subtopic_detail: Heavy bleeding with fever twelve days after birth and echogenic material on scan
stem:
A 26-year-old woman presents on day 12 after a normal vaginal birth with bleeding that has become heavier than her first days at home, soaking one pad every two hours since yesterday. She has felt shivery and her lower abdomen aches.

On examination the uterus is 14 weeks size, soft and tender, and the cervical os admits a fingertip with dark blood and an offensive odour. Pelvic ultrasound shows heterogeneous echogenic material measuring 24 mm within the cavity with vascularity on colour Doppler. She is not bleeding heavily enough in the department to soak a pad while you assess her.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 106/min, BP 108/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 38.3 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 104 g/L (115-165); white cell count 17.2 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0); C-reactive protein 108 mg/L (less than 5)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Immediate surgical evacuation of the uterus in theatre, with antibiotics started afterwards
options.rationale: Instrumenting an acutely infected soft uterus carries a high risk of perforation and of disseminating infection; evacuation is delayed where bleeding allows until antibiotics have taken effect. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guidelines: Postpartum haemorrhage)
source_refs: Queensland Clinical Guidelines: Postpartum haemorrhage

options.text: Oral amoxicillin with clavulanate and outpatient review with a repeat scan in one week
options.rationale: Oral therapy and a week's delay under-treat a woman with fever, tachycardia and marked inflammatory response who needs intravenous cover and close observation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Obstetric and gynaecological infections)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Obstetric and gynaecological infections

options.text: Intramuscular ergometrine with tranexamic acid and discharge once the bleeding has settled
options.rationale: Uterotonics and tranexamic acid may reduce bleeding but do nothing for the infection driving it, and discharge would miss deterioration in a woman with systemic features. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guidelines: Postpartum haemorrhage)
source_refs: Queensland Clinical Guidelines: Postpartum haemorrhage

options.text: Uterine artery embolisation arranged urgently, with antibiotics given once the bleeding stops
options.rationale: Embolisation is for life-threatening haemorrhage unresponsive to medical management, and would leave infected retained tissue in a devascularised uterus. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guidelines: Postpartum haemorrhage)
source_refs: Queensland Clinical Guidelines: Postpartum haemorrhage

options.text: Admit for intravenous antibiotics, with evacuation only if she fails to settle
options.rationale: Intravenous broad-spectrum antibiotics treat the infection first, and evacuation is then performed only if bleeding is heavy or she fails to improve, which minimises perforation and intrauterine adhesion risk. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Obstetric and gynaecological infections)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Obstetric and gynaecological infections
Queensland Clinical Guidelines: Postpartum haemorrhage

explanation.summary: Secondary postpartum haemorrhage, defined as abnormal bleeding between 24 hours and 12 weeks after birth, is usually caused by retained products of conception, endometritis, or both together, and the two are hard to separate clinically. Ultrasound is helpful only in a limited way, since blood clot, decidua and retained tissue all look similar in the first fortnight, and vascularity on Doppler raises but does not confirm retained products. The sequencing principle is that antibiotics precede instrumentation whenever bleeding allows, because a soft infected postpartum uterus perforates easily and curettage at that point also predisposes to intrauterine adhesions. Heavy ongoing bleeding overrides this and forces theatre with antibiotics given concurrently. In context, examine the woman for the other puerperal sources as well, because more than one focus of infection is common.
key_points: Secondary postpartum haemorrhage is bleeding from 24 hours to 12 weeks after birth.
Retained products and endometritis frequently coexist and are hard to separate clinically.
Give intravenous antibiotics before instrumenting the uterus unless bleeding is heavy.
Curettage of an infected soft uterus risks perforation and intrauterine adhesions.
explanation.pearls: Ultrasound after birth cannot reliably distinguish retained products from clot in the first two weeks, so the decision to evacuate is driven by bleeding and by response to antibiotics rather than by the reported endometrial thickness.

subtopic_detail: Negative compression ultrasound with persisting clinical suspicion
stem:
A 32-year-old woman at 27 weeks was started on therapeutic-dose enoxaparin yesterday for three days of left thigh pain and swelling. Compression ultrasound of the femoral and popliteal segments has been reported as showing fully compressible veins with normal flow.

Today the left leg remains 4 cm larger in mid-thigh circumference than the right and she cannot fully bear weight on it. There is no calf erythema, no skin break and she is afebrile. The medical registrar asks whether the enoxaparin can now be stopped.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88/min, BP 114/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius; foetal heart rate 144/min
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 9.4 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0); C-reactive protein 4 mg/L (less than 5); creatinine 51 micromol/L (45-90)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Stop the enoxaparin, as a negative compression ultrasound excludes deep vein thrombosis
options.rationale: A single negative scan does not exclude clot when clinical probability remains high, particularly in pregnancy where the iliac segment is poorly seen and clot may be isolated there. (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: Venous thromboembolism in pregnancy)
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: Venous thromboembolism in pregnancy

options.text: Stop the enoxaparin and send a D-dimer, restarting treatment only if the level is raised
options.rationale: D-dimer rises physiologically through pregnancy and cannot be used to decide whether to continue or stop anticoagulation at any gestation. (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: Venous thromboembolism in pregnancy)
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: Venous thromboembolism in pregnancy

options.text: Stop the enoxaparin and arrange a computed tomography venogram of the pelvis this week
options.rationale: Stopping treatment while further imaging is pending removes cover during the highest-risk interval, and computed tomography venography delivers avoidable pelvic radiation when non-ionising alternatives exist. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guidelines: Venous thromboembolism (VTE) prophylaxis in pregnancy and the puerperium)
source_refs: Queensland Clinical Guidelines: Venous thromboembolism (VTE) prophylaxis in pregnancy and the puerperium

options.text: Continue the enoxaparin and repeat the compression ultrasound within the next three days
options.rationale: With persisting high clinical probability, treatment continues and imaging is repeated, since a calf or iliac clot may only become apparent as it propagates into a visualised segment. (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: Venous thromboembolism in pregnancy)
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: Venous thromboembolism in pregnancy
Queensland Clinical Guidelines: Venous thromboembolism (VTE) prophylaxis in pregnancy and the puerperium

options.text: Continue the enoxaparin and treat empirically for six months without any further leg imaging
options.rationale: Committing a woman to months of injections on suspicion alone, without ever confirming the diagnosis, mislabels her for future pregnancies and contraception decisions. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular - Venous thromboembolism)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular - Venous thromboembolism

explanation.summary: Compression ultrasound in pregnancy has a well-known blind spot: the iliac veins are difficult to compress and difficult to see, particularly on the left where the gravid uterus and the crossing right iliac artery compress the vessel. Isolated iliac thrombosis is therefore the classic missed diagnosis, and it typically presents exactly as here, with whole-leg or thigh swelling and back or buttock pain rather than calf findings. The accepted response to a negative scan with persisting high clinical probability is to continue anticoagulation and repeat imaging within a few days, with magnetic resonance venography reserved for cases where iliac clot is specifically suspected and repeat ultrasound remains negative. Stopping treatment on one negative scan is the error that turns a treatable clot into a fatal embolism. In context, the size of the leg matters more than the confidence of the scan report.
key_points: Compression ultrasound visualises the iliac veins poorly, especially on the left.
Continue anticoagulation and repeat imaging when clinical probability stays high.
Whole-leg or thigh swelling with back or buttock pain suggests iliac vein thrombosis.
Never commit a woman to long-term anticoagulation without confirming the diagnosis.
explanation.pearls: Left iliofemoral thrombosis accounts for the majority of pregnancy deep vein thrombosis, and the pattern of proximal swelling with a normal-looking calf is the clue that the clot sits above where the probe can compress.

subtopic_detail: Collapse with rash two days after repair of a high vaginal tear
stem:
A 25-year-old woman is reviewed on the postnatal ward two days after a vacuum birth complicated by a high vaginal tear that was repaired in theatre. She has vomited three times this morning, had two loose motions, and feels dizzy when she sits up.

She is flushed with a diffuse red blanching rash over her trunk and limbs and her conjunctivae are injected. Her abdomen is soft with a well contracted non-tender uterus, and her breasts and caesarean-free abdomen are unremarkable. The theatre record notes that a vaginal pack was inserted at the end of the repair, and there is no entry in the notes recording its removal.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 132/min, BP 84/46 mmHg, respiratory rate 28/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 39.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 21.8 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0); C-reactive protein 186 mg/L (less than 5); lactate 4.4 mmol/L (less than 2.0); creatinine 148 micromol/L (45-90); platelets 88 x10^9/L (150-400)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Intravenous fluid resuscitation and broad-spectrum antibiotics, with the vaginal examination deferred
options.rationale: Resuscitation and antibiotics are both necessary, but leaving the source in place means the toxin-producing focus continues to drive the shock; source control cannot be deferred. (Source: Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care: Sepsis Clinical Care Standard)
source_refs: Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care: Sepsis Clinical Care Standard

options.text: Vaginal examination and pack removal, with fluid resuscitation and intravenous antibiotics
options.rationale: Removing the retained foreign body is the source control step, and it is done alongside rather than after resuscitation and antibiotic administration in a woman who is already shocked. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Sepsis and septic shock)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Sepsis and septic shock
Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care: Sepsis Clinical Care Standard

options.text: Intravenous hydrocortisone and antihistamine, with observation for progression of the rash
options.rationale: This treats the presentation as an allergic reaction, but the fever, raised lactate, renal impairment and inflammatory response point to infection rather than anaphylaxis or drug eruption. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guidelines: Sepsis in pregnancy and the puerperium)
source_refs: Queensland Clinical Guidelines: Sepsis in pregnancy and the puerperium

options.text: Computed tomography of the abdomen and pelvis before any vaginal examination is done
options.rationale: Imaging delays both resuscitation and source control in a shocked woman, and would not add to a bedside examination that can identify and remove the focus immediately. (Source: Clinical Excellence Commission (NSW): SEPSIS KILLS program)
source_refs: Clinical Excellence Commission (NSW): SEPSIS KILLS program

options.text: Intravenous fluconazole with antibiotic cover, pending blood and high vaginal swab results
options.rationale: Empirical antifungal therapy is not part of initial management of puerperal sepsis and does not address the retained foreign body that is driving the illness. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Sepsis and septic shock)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Sepsis and septic shock

explanation.summary: Toxin-mediated shock from a retained vaginal foreign body is rare but is one of the few postnatal sepsis presentations where the treatment is at the bedside rather than in the pharmacy. The picture is a very rapid onset of fever, hypotension, vomiting and diarrhoea, a diffuse blanching erythroderma with mucosal involvement, and multi-organ derangement including renal impairment and thrombocytopenia, often with a uterus that examines normally. Recognition depends on reading the operative record, because the woman herself will frequently not know a pack was left. Management is simultaneous rather than sequential: resuscitate, take cultures, give antibiotics within the hour, and remove the source. In context, every unit should have an explicit pack count and removal entry, and an unclosed entry is itself a red flag when a postnatal woman deteriorates.
key_points: Suspect a retained foreign body when postnatal shock follows an operative vaginal repair.
Diffuse blanching erythroderma with vomiting, diarrhoea and organ dysfunction suggests a toxin-mediated illness.
Source control happens alongside resuscitation and antibiotics, not after them.
Read the operative record for pack insertion when a postnatal woman deteriorates unexpectedly.
explanation.pearls: Desquamation of the palms and soles appears one to two weeks after the acute illness in toxin-mediated shock, which is far too late to help with the diagnosis but confirms it retrospectively.

subtopic_detail: Persisting fever on adequate antibiotics after caesarean with a vascular filling defect
stem:
A 29-year-old woman is day 7 after an emergency caesarean and has been on intravenous ampicillin, gentamicin and metronidazole for 72 hours for a uterine infection. Her abdominal pain has improved and her lochia is no longer offensive, but she continues to spike to 38.8 degrees Celsius twice daily.

Her wound is clean and dry, her chest is clear, her calves are soft and equal and her urine culture is negative. Blood cultures taken before antibiotics grew nothing. Computed tomography of the abdomen and pelvis with contrast reports no collection and no retained products, but describes an enlarged right ovarian vein containing a low-attenuation filling defect extending toward the inferior vena cava.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 102/min, BP 112/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 38.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 15.4 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0); C-reactive protein 96 mg/L (less than 5); blood and urine cultures negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate addition to her management?

options.text: Add therapeutic anticoagulation to the current course of intravenous antibiotic therapy
options.rationale: A septic thrombus in the ovarian vein explains fever that persists despite adequate antibiotics, and treatment requires anticoagulation alongside continued antibiotic therapy rather than a change of antibiotic. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Obstetric and gynaecological infections)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Obstetric and gynaecological infections
Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: Venous thromboembolism in pregnancy

options.text: Change to intravenous meropenem and add vancomycin to cover resistant hospital organisms
options.rationale: Escalating the spectrum is the reflex response to persistent fever, but her abdominal signs and lochia are improving and the cultures are negative, so a resistant organism is not the best explanation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Obstetric and gynaecological infections)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Obstetric and gynaecological infections

options.text: Proceed to laparotomy for washout and possible hysterectomy given the failure to defervesce
options.rationale: Surgical source control is for a drainable collection, necrotic tissue or a uterus that cannot be salvaged; imaging has excluded a collection and she is clinically improving in every respect except temperature. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guidelines: Sepsis in pregnancy and the puerperium)
source_refs: Queensland Clinical Guidelines: Sepsis in pregnancy and the puerperium

options.text: Add intravenous fluconazole for possible candidaemia after a week of broad-spectrum therapy
options.rationale: Empirical antifungal therapy is considered in immunosuppressed or intensive care patients with persistent fever, and would not explain a discrete vascular abnormality on imaging. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Sepsis and septic shock)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Sepsis and septic shock

options.text: Cease antibiotics and repeat the computed tomography in 48 hours to reassess
options.rationale: Stopping antibiotics in a woman who is still febrile with a raised inflammatory response risks relapse of the uterine infection, and repeat imaging will not change a diagnosis already made. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Obstetric and gynaecological infections)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Obstetric and gynaecological infections

explanation.summary: Septic thrombophlebitis of the pelvic veins is the classic explanation for a woman who remains febrile after caesarean despite appropriate antibiotics while otherwise improving. It arises when endometrial infection seeds the venous plexus, most often the right ovarian vein, because dextrorotation of the uterus and antegrade flow favour that side. Contrast computed tomography or magnetic resonance venography shows an enlarged vein with a filling defect and surrounding inflammatory change. Treatment is anticoagulation added to continued antibiotics, with most women defervescing within 48 to 72 hours; the optimal duration of anticoagulation is not well established and is usually decided with haematology input. In context, this diagnosis sits exactly on the boundary between the two leading direct causes of maternal death, infection and clot, and is missed when persistent fever is treated only by escalating the antibiotic.
key_points: Consider pelvic vein septic thrombophlebitis when fever persists despite adequate antibiotics.
The right ovarian vein is the usual site because of uterine dextrorotation and flow direction.
Diagnosis is by contrast computed tomography or magnetic resonance venography.
Treatment adds anticoagulation to antibiotics rather than broadening antibiotic cover.
explanation.pearls: Defervescence within 48 to 72 hours of starting anticoagulation supports the diagnosis of septic pelvic vein thrombophlebitis, since no antibiotic change has been made.

subtopic_detail: Thromboprophylaxis the day after a transfused major postpartum haemorrhage
stem:
A 37-year-old woman is day 1 after an emergency caesarean at full dilatation. She lost 1900 mL, received three units of red cells and one gram of tranexamic acid, and had a balloon tamponade device removed at 12 hours with no further loss.

Her booking weight was 78 kg and her body mass index at booking was 29. Graduated compression stockings have been in place since theatre. Since the balloon came out her uterus has stayed firm, her pad loss has been minimal and her abdominal drain has drained 30 mL over eight hours. She has not yet been out of bed and is asking when she can start walking.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 94/min, BP 112/66 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 82 g/L (115-165); platelets 142 x10^9/L (150-400); fibrinogen 2.9 g/L (2.0-4.5); international normalised ratio 1.1 (0.8-1.2); creatinine 62 micromol/L (45-90)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate venous thromboembolism prevention plan?

options.text: Withhold heparin until her haemoglobin rises above 100 g/L, using stockings meanwhile
options.rationale: Anaemia after a treated haemorrhage is not a bleeding risk factor in itself, and tying prophylaxis to a haemoglobin target has no basis in any Australian risk assessment tool. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guidelines: Venous thromboembolism (VTE) prophylaxis in pregnancy and the puerperium)
source_refs: Queensland Clinical Guidelines: Venous thromboembolism (VTE) prophylaxis in pregnancy and the puerperium

options.text: Withhold heparin for seven days after major haemorrhage, using mechanical measures alone
options.rationale: A week of mechanical prophylaxis alone spans the period of peak thrombotic risk in a woman with several strong risk factors, and no guideline mandates such a delay once bleeding has stopped. (Source: Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care: Venous Thromboembolism Prevention Clinical Care Standard)
source_refs: Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care: Venous Thromboembolism Prevention Clinical Care Standard

options.text: Start prophylactic-dose enoxaparin today and continue the mechanical measures as well
options.rationale: Transfused haemorrhage is itself a strong thrombotic risk factor, her coagulation profile and platelets are adequate and there is no ongoing bleeding, so prophylaxis should begin rather than be deferred. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guidelines: Venous thromboembolism (VTE) prophylaxis in pregnancy and the puerperium)
source_refs: Queensland Clinical Guidelines: Venous thromboembolism (VTE) prophylaxis in pregnancy and the puerperium
Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care: Venous Thromboembolism Prevention Clinical Care Standard

options.text: Start treatment-dose enoxaparin now, given the number of thrombotic risk factors accrued
options.rationale: Treatment intensity is for a diagnosed clot; using it as prophylaxis the day after a transfused haemorrhage adds bleeding risk without evidence of benefit. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Enoxaparin)
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook: Enoxaparin

options.text: Give aspirin 100 mg daily until she is mobile, then convert to enoxaparin
options.rationale: Aspirin is substantially less effective than heparin for venous prophylaxis and confers its own bleeding risk on a fresh surgical wound. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular - Venous thromboembolism)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular - Venous thromboembolism

explanation.summary: Major postpartum haemorrhage sets a trap: it is both a strong risk factor for venous thromboembolism and an intuitive reason to withhold anticoagulation, and the intuition frequently wins on ward rounds. Australian risk assessment tools score blood loss above 1000 mL or transfusion as a significant thrombotic risk factor, alongside caesarean in labour, age over 35, raised body mass index and immobility, which this woman also has. The genuine contraindications are active bleeding, a platelet count below roughly 75 x10^9/L, uncorrected coagulopathy, and a recent or planned neuraxial procedure within the timing window. Once haemostasis has been achieved and the coagulation profile is adequate, prophylaxis should begin, typically within 6 to 12 hours of surgery or once the bleeding has stopped. In context, deaths from postnatal pulmonary embolism repeatedly involve women in whom prophylaxis was deferred for a bleeding risk that had already resolved.
key_points: Transfused haemorrhage is a thrombotic risk factor, not a standing contraindication to prophylaxis.
Genuine contraindications are active bleeding, platelets below about 75 x10^9/L and uncorrected coagulopathy.
Start prophylaxis once haemostasis is secure, usually within 6 to 12 hours of surgery.
Anaemia alone does not justify withholding heparin prophylaxis.
explanation.pearls: Balloon tamponade for haemorrhage does not by itself contraindicate heparin: prophylaxis is generally started once the device is out and loss has settled, rather than being deferred to discharge.

subtopic_detail: Selecting the enoxaparin dose band after caesarean when weight has changed
stem:
A 34-year-old woman is on the ward the morning after an emergency caesarean at 39 weeks for failure to progress. She is well, her wound is dry, her uterus is firm and her pad loss is light, and you are asked to prescribe her thromboprophylaxis before the ward round moves on.

Her first antenatal visit at 11 weeks recorded a weight of 88 kg. She gained weight steadily through the pregnancy and her weight on the ward scales this morning, after 3 litres of intraoperative and postoperative fluid, is 104 kg with pitting oedema to mid-shin. She is on no other anticoagulant and has had no bleeding since theatre.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 86/min, BP 116/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: Platelets 218 x10^9/L (150-400); creatinine 58 micromol/L (45-90); haemoglobin 108 g/L (115-165)

lead_in: Which prophylactic enoxaparin regimen would you prescribe?

options.text: Enoxaparin 20 mg subcutaneously daily, reflecting her low bleeding risk after an uncomplicated operation
options.rationale: The 20 mg band applies to women below 50 kg; using it here would under-dose her substantially at the point of her highest thrombotic risk. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guidelines: Venous thromboembolism (VTE) prophylaxis in pregnancy and the puerperium)
source_refs: Queensland Clinical Guidelines: Venous thromboembolism (VTE) prophylaxis in pregnancy and the puerperium

options.text: Enoxaparin 60 mg subcutaneously daily, calculated from the weight recorded on the ward scales today
options.rationale: Today's weight includes 3 litres of administered fluid and oedema, which inflates it into the next band; dosing tables are built on early pregnancy weight for exactly this reason. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guidelines: Venous thromboembolism (VTE) prophylaxis in pregnancy and the puerperium)
source_refs: Queensland Clinical Guidelines: Venous thromboembolism (VTE) prophylaxis in pregnancy and the puerperium

options.text: Enoxaparin 80 mg subcutaneously daily, calculated from her weight plus total pregnancy weight gain
options.rationale: The 80 mg band is for women in the 131 to 170 kg range, and adding gestational weight gain to a current weight double-counts the same kilograms. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guidelines: Venous thromboembolism (VTE) prophylaxis in pregnancy and the puerperium)
source_refs: Queensland Clinical Guidelines: Venous thromboembolism (VTE) prophylaxis in pregnancy and the puerperium

options.text: Enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneously twice daily, reflecting her caesarean birth and her body mass index
options.rationale: Twice-daily prophylactic dosing is used in some very high body weight or high-risk protocols, not as a routine response to caesarean birth in a woman within the standard band. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Enoxaparin)
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook: Enoxaparin

options.text: Enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneously daily, calculated from the weight recorded at her booking visit
options.rationale: Prophylactic dose bands in the Australian maternity tables are set by booking weight, and 88 kg sits in the 50 to 90 kg band, which attracts 40 mg daily. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guidelines: Venous thromboembolism (VTE) prophylaxis in pregnancy and the puerperium)
source_refs: Queensland Clinical Guidelines: Venous thromboembolism (VTE) prophylaxis in pregnancy and the puerperium
Australian Medicines Handbook: Enoxaparin

explanation.summary: Weight-banded prophylactic enoxaparin dosing in maternity is built on booking weight rather than on current weight, because a term or immediately postnatal weight is inflated by the products of conception, by physiological plasma volume expansion and by any fluid given around the birth. Using the inflated figure pushes many women up a band and exposes them to unnecessary bleeding risk, while using an arbitrary fixed dose under-treats the heaviest women. The commonly used bands are 20 mg daily below 50 kg, 40 mg daily for 50 to 90 kg, 60 mg daily for 91 to 130 kg, 80 mg daily for 131 to 170 kg, and weight-calculated dosing above that. Renal impairment requires separate dose adjustment, which is why creatinine is checked before prescribing. In context, the woman closest to a band boundary is the one where the choice of weight actually changes the prescription, and that is where this error is made.
key_points: Prophylactic enoxaparin dose bands in maternity are set by booking weight.
Postnatal weight is inflated by fluid, oedema and physiological volume expansion.
Standard bands are 20 mg, 40 mg, 60 mg and 80 mg daily across ascending weight ranges.
Check renal function before prescribing, as impairment requires separate adjustment.
explanation.pearls: Enoxaparin is cleared renally, so a creatinine clearance below 30 mL/min requires dose reduction or a switch to unfractionated heparin even when the weight band would otherwise be straightforward.

subtopic_detail: Perineal pain out of proportion with a normal temperature two days after birth
stem:
A 28-year-old woman is called to your attention on day 2 after a forceps birth with a repaired third-degree tear. She has needed escalating oxycodone overnight and is now asking for more, saying the pain is nothing like the soreness she remembers from her first birth. She is drowsy and slow to answer questions.

The perineum looks moderately swollen with a dusky area of discolouration extending toward the right labium majus and a small amount of thin grey discharge from the repair. Tenderness extends well beyond the visible discolouration onto the right inner thigh, and a patch of skin over the labium is numb to light touch. Her temperature is 36.1 degrees Celsius and she has had no rigors.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 128/min, BP 86/48 mmHg, respiratory rate 30/min, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 36.1 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 24.6 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0); C-reactive protein 268 mg/L (less than 5); lactate 4.8 mmol/L (less than 2.0); creatinine 156 micromol/L (45-90); sodium 128 mmol/L (135-145)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Intravenous antibiotics with fluid resuscitation and reassessment of the perineum in six hours
options.rationale: Antibiotics do not penetrate thrombosed necrotic tissue, and a six hour observation period in a woman with this degree of organ dysfunction allows the infection to advance along fascial planes. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Necrotising skin and soft tissue infections)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Necrotising skin and soft tissue infections

options.text: Bedside incision and drainage of the perineal wound with swabs and oral antibiotics
options.rationale: Ward drainage is appropriate for a localised collection, but here the disease extends well beyond the wound and requires formal exploration with excision of all non-viable tissue. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guidelines: Perineal care)
source_refs: Queensland Clinical Guidelines: Perineal care
Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Necrotising skin and soft tissue infections

options.text: Magnetic resonance imaging of the perineum before referral for a surgical opinion
options.rationale: Imaging may show fascial oedema or gas but is never allowed to delay theatre in a shocked woman, and a normal study does not exclude the diagnosis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Necrotising skin and soft tissue infections)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Necrotising skin and soft tissue infections

options.text: Immediate theatre for exploration and debridement, with urgent resuscitation and antibiotics
options.rationale: Pain out of proportion, extension beyond the visible margins, cutaneous anaesthesia and organ dysfunction indicate necrotising soft tissue infection, where survival depends on early and complete surgical debridement alongside resuscitation and antibiotics. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Necrotising skin and soft tissue infections)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Necrotising skin and soft tissue infections
Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care: Sepsis Clinical Care Standard

options.text: Intravenous flucloxacillin with a wound swab and stronger analgesia, reviewed on rounds
options.rationale: Single-agent antistaphylococcal therapy is inadequate for a polymicrobial or group A streptococcal necrotising infection, and increasing analgesia treats the cardinal warning sign rather than its cause. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Skin and soft tissue infections)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Skin and soft tissue infections

explanation.summary: Necrotising soft tissue infection of the perineum after childbirth is rare, rapidly fatal and easy to mislabel as ordinary wound infection, particularly because perineal pain and swelling are expected after an instrumental birth with a third-degree tear. The features that should override the default reading are pain far out of proportion to the visible findings, tenderness extending beyond the erythema, skin anaesthesia from destruction of cutaneous nerves, thin grey discharge, and systemic toxicity. Fever may be absent or the woman may be frankly hypothermic, and a normal temperature is one of the commonest reasons the diagnosis is delayed. Group A streptococcus is a major cause of maternal death from genital tract sepsis in Australia and can produce this picture within hours. In context, the definitive treatment is surgical: antibiotics and resuscitation support the operation but never replace it.
key_points: Pain out of proportion with tenderness beyond the visible margins is the cardinal early sign.
Cutaneous anaesthesia and thin grey discharge point to fascial plane involvement.
Normal temperature or hypothermia does not exclude severe sepsis and often delays diagnosis.
Early complete surgical debridement is the intervention that determines survival.
explanation.pearls: Hyponatraemia with a white cell count above 15 x10^9/L in a soft tissue infection is a recognised laboratory warning pattern for necrotising infection and should prompt surgical review rather than another dose of antibiotic.
